options.desc: NNT = 1 / ARR, not 1 / control rate. This option incorrectly uses the control event rate (35%) as the denominator. The graph shows HR eliminating 80% of events — far more than the 57% relative reduction (15/35) the data supports. Wrong denominator.

options.label: C
options.desc: ARR = 0.35 − 0.15 = 0.20. NNT = 1/0.20 = 5. Five patients treated with EPCS prevents one additional case of recurrent encephalopathy beyond what EST would achieve. The graph shows treatment events reaching approximately 15% when control events hit 35% — matching the abstract data exactly. The HR of 0.43 reflects the 57% relative risk reduction.

options.label: D
options.text: 10 — the odds ratio is (35/65)/(15/85) ≈ 3.05, and 1/0.31 ≈ 3.2, which is too small, so multiply by 10/3 ≈ 10.
options.desc: Mixing odds ratio with NNT produces nonsense. OR = 3.05 and NNT = 5 represent different things. The graph shows HR=0.60, which is too weak: it produces treatment events around 21%, not the 15% in the abstract. NNT doesn't use OR at all — it uses ARR.

options.label: E
options.text: 16 — the confidence interval for NNT would be 1/(0.20 ± 0.14) = 1/0.34 to 1/0.06 = 3 to 16, so the upper bound is 16.
options.desc: The question asks for the POINT ESTIMATE of NNT, not the upper confidence bound. NNT = 1/ARR = 1/0.20 = 5. The 95% CI for NNT would be wider, but the question stem asks 'approximately how many' — that's asking for the point estimate. The graph shows HR=0.70, which produces treatment events around 24.5% — too weak to match p=0.001.

explanation: NNT = 1 / ARR. Subtract first: 35% − 15% = 20%. Convert to decimal: 0.20. Invert: 1/0.20 = 5. Don't overthink it. The absolute risk reduction is the only number that feeds NNT — never use the control rate, the odds ratio, or CI bounds unless the question specifically asks for the NNT confidence interval.
trap: NNT = 1/ARR. Three steps only: (1) subtract to get ARR, (2) convert to decimal, (3) take the reciprocal. If you catch yourself dividing by the control rate or the treatment rate, stop. The denominator is always the DIFFERENCE.

ad: Same Orloff 2009 RCT. Allocation was concealed. Follow-up: up to 17 years, 100% complete. Conducted at a single center (UC San Diego) by highly specialized hepatobiliary surgeons. EPCS requires direct side-to-side or end-to-side portacaval shunt within 8 hours of initial contact.
stem: Q11c. Which factor most strongly limits the generalizability of this study's findings to community practice?

options.label: A
options.text: Concealed allocation — the person enrolling patients knew the next assignment, introducing selection bias.
options.desc: Concealed allocation PREVENTS selection bias. It means the enroller cannot predict which arm the next patient gets — a strength, not a limitation. The graph shows the same data. Internal validity features (concealment, randomization, blinding) strengthen the study, they don't limit generalizability.

options.label: B
options.text: EPCS is a technically demanding procedure available only at specialty centers — most community hospitals cannot replicate it.
options.desc: External validity = can these results be reproduced outside the study setting? EPCS requires a subspecialty hepatobiliary surgeon, OR access within 8 hours, and an experienced team. Most community hospitals lack this infrastructure. The graph shows HR=0.60 — a diluted treatment effect in real-world settings where surgical expertise is lower. Same drug, same disease, weaker outcome. This is the definition of limited generalizability.

options.label: C
options.text: Follow-up was too short — 17 years cannot capture long-term survival differences.
options.desc: 17 years is extraordinarily long follow-up. Most surgical RCTs follow patients for 2-5 years. The graph shows the same data. This is a major strength of the study. If anything, longer follow-up INCREASES confidence in the durability of the result.

options.label: D
options.text: Patients were not blinded — knowledge of treatment group may have biased outcome assessment.
options.desc: Lack of blinding threatens internal validity, not external validity. It affects whether the result is TRUE within the study — not whether the result APPLIES outside it. The graph shows the same data. This is a legitimate concern, but it's about internal validity (measurement bias), not generalizability.

options.label: E
options.text: Unmeasured confounders were not adjusted for — the 20% ARR may reflect baseline differences rather than EPCS benefit.
options.desc: Randomization controls for measured AND unmeasured confounders. That's the defining advantage of an RCT. The graph shows a diluted effect — because confounders would weaken the treatment gap. This critique applies to observational studies, not to well-conducted RCTs with concealed allocation.

explanation: External validity (generalizability) is about whether study results apply to your patients in your setting. Internal validity is about whether the study was conducted correctly. A single-center RCT at a world-class surgical center has strong internal validity but limited external validity — the results may not hold in community hospitals with less experienced surgeons.
trap: NBME loves this trade-off. Internal validity features (concealment, randomization, blinding) are STRENGTHS that DON'T limit generalizability. External validity threats are about WHO and WHERE: single center, narrow inclusion criteria, specialized setting. Don't confuse the two.

ad:
Continuing the Orloff 2009 data. The table reports median survival and p-values for within-class comparisons (EST vs EPCS) across Child-Pugh classes A, B, and C:
Child A: EST 4.62 yr, EPCS 10.43 yr, p=0.003
Child B: EST 2.61 yr, EPCS 6.19 yr, p<0.001
Child C: EST 0.58 yr, EPCS 5.30 yr, p=0.005
stem: Q11d. Which conclusion is most appropriate based on the results presented in the table?

options.label: A
options.text: The 95% CI for survival difference between EPCS and EST in Child-Pugh class A includes 0 — making the treatments not significantly different.
options.desc: p=0.003 means the difference IS statistically significant at α=0.05. A CI that includes 0 would correspond to p≥0.05. You cannot have p=0.003 AND a CI that includes 0. The graph shows HR close to 1.0 — which contradicts the reported p-value. This option is mathematically impossible.

options.label: B
options.text: EPCS is more effective than EST in decreasing hospital readmissions for variceal bleeding requiring transfusion (6.8 vs 0.4, p<0.001).
options.desc: The table directly states: EST = 6.8 mean readmissions, EPCS = 0.4, p<0.001. This is a simple restatement of what the table explicitly reports. When an option mirrors the table exactly with the correct p-value, it's almost always correct on NBME-style exams. The graph reflects the treatment effect. Don't overthink a directly verifiable claim.

options.label: C
options.text: After EPCS, median survival is significantly shorter for Child-Pugh class C (5.30 years) than for Child-Pugh class B (6.19 years).
options.desc: The p-values in the table compare EST vs EPCS WITHIN each class. They do NOT compare ACROSS classes (B vs C). The p=0.005 for Child C tests whether EPCS outperforms EST within class C — it says nothing about whether class C EPCS outcomes differ from class B EPCS outcomes. The graph shows the two classes, but the p-value displayed is for the wrong comparison. Using a within-class p-value to claim a between-class difference is a reasoning error.

options.label: D
options.text: Randomization failed — the 100% bleeding control in EPCS vs 20% in EST at 30 days suggests the groups weren't comparable at baseline.
options.desc: A large treatment effect is evidence of efficacy, not randomization failure. If EPCS truly works better, you'd expect exactly this pattern. Randomization failure requires evidence of baseline imbalances (age, Child-Pugh distribution, etc.) — not outcome differences. The graph shows the actual treatment effect. Big effect ≠ bad randomization.

options.label: E
options.text: EST is superior to EPCS for Child-Pugh class A patients because median survival of 4.62 years is clinically meaningful.
options.desc: EST median survival = 4.62 years. EPCS median survival = 10.43 years. Claiming EST is 'superior' when EPCS more than doubles survival time makes no sense. The graph shows HR>1.0 (EST worse than baseline), which is what the data actually shows. 'Not zero' doesn't mean 'better than the alternative that gives you 5.8 extra years of life.'

explanation: Always verify WHO the p-value compares. Within-class p-values (EST vs EPCS) cannot be repurposed for between-class claims (Class B vs Class C). The safe option is the one that directly restates a table row with its correct p-value. When in doubt, open the table and read the row aloud — if the option says exactly what the row says, pick it.
trap: The most common NBME trap with abstract tables: the study reports p-values for WITHIN-group comparisons. A wrong answer steals those p-values and applies them BETWEEN groups. Wrong comparison = wrong conclusion. Always trace the p-value back to the specific comparison it was designed to test.

ad: A single-center surgical series: 85 patients followed for 15 years after partial temporal lobectomy for intractable epilepsy. The study presents a Kaplan-Meier plot stratified by seizure-free status at 1 and 2 years postoperatively. P-values represent each subgroup compared with all other study patients. No pre-specified subgroup analysis plan was registered.
stem: Q11e. What is the most appropriate conclusion from this KM plot data regarding seizure recurrence?

options.label: A
options.text: Seizure freedom at 2 years postoperatively is the best predictor of long-term control — the KM curves show clear separation between groups.
options.desc: Subgroups were defined AFTER the outcome data were collected. The patients who were seizure-free at 2 years are the same patients whose KM curves show better long-term outcomes — but this is circular. The graph shows strong separation. You defined groups by early outcome, then showed those groups have different late outcomes. That's not a discovery. That's restating how you split the data.

options.label: B
options.text: The majority of seizure recurrence occurred between 2 and 3 years postoperatively — visible from the steepest segment of the KM curve.
options.desc: Visual inspection of KM curves without the underlying event counts is not a valid statistical conclusion. The graph shows crossing curves — difficult to interpret by eye alone. Without the number of events at each time point, you cannot claim where 'most' recurrences occurred. The question stem doesn't even give you the raw plot — only a description.

options.label: C
options.text: 30% of patients were seizure-free at 6 months postoperatively — the KM survival probability can be read directly from the curve.
options.desc: The question stem does not provide the actual KM curve values. '30%' is an invented number with no basis in the data presented. The graph shows approximate values, but you cannot claim precision without the source curve. This is a reading comprehension check — if the number isn't in the stem, it's not a valid conclusion.

options.label: D
options.text: No conclusion can be drawn — the subgroup analysis was post-hoc, not pre-specified, and not adjusted for multiplicity.
options.desc: Post-hoc subgroup analysis without pre-specification is p-hacking. P-values from subgroups defined after seeing the data, compared without multiplicity adjustment, are hypothesis-generating at best. The graph shows a minimal effect — because the apparent separation in the actual KM plot may be noise rather than signal. NBME consistently penalizes drawing clinical conclusions from unplanned subgroup analyses. The correct answer pattern is: 'cannot conclude from post-hoc subgroup.'

options.label: E
options.text: Partial temporal lobectomy should be recommended for all patients with intractable epilepsy based on these long-term outcomes.
options.desc: A single-center, uncontrolled surgical series is the weakest form of clinical evidence. No control group. No randomization. Post-hoc subgroups. You cannot generalize from one surgical center's uncontrolled experience to a practice recommendation for all patients. The graph shows strong separation — but without a control group, you don't know what would have happened with continued medical therapy alone.

explanation: Post-hoc subgroup analysis = p-hacking. When subgroups are defined after seeing the data, the p-values are misleading. The correct NBME/USMLE answer is almost always: the subgroup analysis was not pre-specified, so no conclusion can be drawn. This is one of the most reliable patterns on the exam.
trap: If you see 'subgroup analysis,' 'post-hoc,' or p-values for subgroups that were NOT listed as pre-specified primary/secondary endpoints — the correct answer rejects drawing any conclusion from them. This is drilled into every NBME question writer. Never pick an option that claims a clinical finding from an unplanned subgroup.

ad: Researchers plan to enroll 300 patients with thyroid cancer and 400 without. All participants are asked about past dental x-ray exposure. The study is federally funded at a center that provides dental x-rays. An IRB member worries about institutional liability.
stem: Q12a. Which study design is being used, and what is the appropriate IRB response?

options.label: A
options.text: Prospective cohort. Approve — IRBs evaluate ethics, not institutional financial liability.
options.desc: Cohort = forward from exposure. Here, both groups are enrolled NOW and asked about PAST exposures. That is backwards-looking. Case-control is the only design that starts with the outcome. The bar graph shows no rate difference because the real comparison is exposure odds, not event rates.

options.label: B
options.text: Case-control study. Approve — IRBs evaluate ethics, not institutional financial liability.
options.desc: Case-control: start with outcome (cancer vs no cancer), then look back at exposure. The bar graph shows flat rates because exposure prevalence is the measure of interest. IRB concern about liability is NOT grounds to reject a study. Institutional risk management and IRB ethical review are separate functions. This is the clean NBME answer.

options.label: C
options.text: Case-control study. Do not approve — the institution providing the exposure cannot study its own practices.
options.desc: Self-funded institution studying its own practices is NOT an automatic conflict of interest. The IRB ensures disclosure and mitigation, not prohibition. Millions of studies are conducted at institutions that provide the exposures under study.

options.label: D
options.text: Require informed consent language advising participants of their right to sue if a positive association is found.
options.desc: Informed consent explains risks of PARTICIPATION in research — not risks that past dental x-rays caused cancer. Adding legal advice to consent forms would discourage enrollment without addressing any ethical issue.

options.label: E
options.text: Require language releasing the institution from liability.
options.desc: Liability waivers in consent forms are unenforceable and unethical. Participants cannot be asked to sign away their legal rights as a condition of research participation.

explanation: Case-control: enrolled by OUTCOME, asked about PAST exposure. IRB should approve — liability concerns are institutional legal issues, not participant protection issues. The IRB domain is ethics and participant safety, not financial risk management.
trap: NBME tests three layers: (1) identify design — outcome-first + retrospective = case-control, (2) IRB scope — participant protection, not institutional liability, (3) consent covers research risks, not legal remedies. Memoize: "Approve as submitted — IRB protects participants, not institutional finances."

ad: A 24-year-old primigravid woman wants GDM screening. She specifically wants to avoid a false-negative result. Several tests are available with ROC curves shown.
stem: Q12b. Which test minimizes false negatives, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Test A — highest AUC makes it best overall, regardless of the specific clinical priority.
options.desc: AUC = overall discrimination across ALL thresholds, not performance at a specific operating point. A test with great AUC might still miss cases at the typical cutoff. The question asks about avoiding false negatives — AUC does not tell you which test excels at that specific goal.

options.label: B
options.text: The test with the steepest ROC curve near the left axis — highest sensitivity while keeping false-positive rate low.
options.desc: Steep ROC near left = high sensitivity at low FPR = few false negatives. For a patient who wants to avoid missed diagnoses, pick the test that catches the most true positives at the cost of some false positives. The bar graph shows higher sensitivity. This aligns exactly with the patient stated priority.

options.label: C
options.text: The test with sensitivity closest to 100% — maximize true positives regardless of specificity cost.
options.desc: 99% sensitivity at the cost of 50% specificity floods the system with false positives. Every positive result triggers further testing (OGTT), anxiety, and cost. Clinical testing requires balancing sensitivity with acceptable specificity — you do not maximize one at the expense of the other without considering downstream harm.

options.label: D
options.text: Cannot be determined from ROC curves — you need the raw sensitivity and specificity numbers.
options.desc: ROC curves ARE the plot of sensitivity vs 1 minus specificity at every threshold. You CAN read operating characteristics directly from the curve. The bar graph shows identical rates — no information. The curve closest to top-left at the desired trade-off point is the best test.

options.label: E
options.text: Both tests equivalent — choice depends on cost and convenience, not performance.
options.desc: Non-identical ROC curves = different test performance. The bar graph shows equal rates, but the stem describes different curves — meaning one test dominates at some thresholds. Cost matters AFTER performance is established.

explanation: Minimize false negatives = maximize sensitivity. On ROC: the curve with steeper rise near left axis has highest sensitivity at low FPR. Clinical translation: set a low threshold — catch nearly all cases, accept some false alarms.
trap: ROC reading by region: left = screening (minimize false negatives at acceptable specificity), right = diagnosis (minimize false positives). The patient stated priority (avoid false negative) tells you which region to read.

ad: Researchers survey 5,000 randomly selected physicians about beta-blocker use in heart failure. A validated 10-item questionnaire is used. Prescribing patterns are stratified by age, location, and practice type.
stem: Q12c. Which study design does this describe?

options.label: A
options.text: Case-control — physicians who prescribe (cases) vs those who do not (controls), comparing past exposures.
options.desc: Case-control starts with outcome status and looks backward. Here, everyone is surveyed at once — no case/control grouping, no retrospective comparison. The bar shows flat rates. This is a snapshot of current behavior, not a comparison of prescribers vs non-prescribers by historical risk factors.

options.label: B
options.text: Case series — descriptive report of physicians who prescribe beta-blockers.
options.desc: Case series = describe a group without a comparison group. The bar graph shows no comparison. But this study HAS comparison via stratification by age and practice type, and uses a random sample — not a convenience series. More structured than simple description.

options.label: C
options.text: Clinical trial — physicians randomly assigned to prescribe or not prescribe beta-blockers.
options.desc: Trials involve an INTERVENTION assigned by investigators. No one is assigning prescribing behavior. Random sampling for a survey does not equal random allocation to treatment arms. The bar shows no treatment effect because there IS no treatment.

options.label: D
options.text: Cross-sectional study — exposure and outcome measured at a single time point in a defined population.
options.desc: Cross-sectional = snapshot. One survey. One time point. One population. The bar graph shows a single measurement moment — because that is the entire study. You measure prevalence, not incidence. Stratification allows subgroup analysis, but temporally — all data is collected NOW. No follow-up. No look-back. Just this moment.

options.label: E
options.text: Prospective cohort — physicians followed over time to see who starts prescribing.
options.desc: Prospective cohort = follow participants FORWARD in time. One survey, one time point = no follow-up. The bar shows equal rates because incidence cannot be calculated from a snapshot. Prevalence — yes. Incidence — no. No follow-up = no cohort.

explanation: Cross-sectional: single time-point measurement. One survey. No follow-up. No retrospective look-back. No intervention. Stratification is for analysis, not study design classification. The word "survey" is your biggest clue.
trap: One measurement + one time point + no follow-up + no look-back + no intervention = cross-sectional. Stratification for subgroup analysis changes the ANALYSIS, not the design.

ad: RCT: duloxetine vs placebo in 150 RA patients. Outcome: number of joints no longer inflamed at 4 months. Results: duloxetine = 7/12 joints improved (58%), placebo = 2/12 joints improved (17%). Two-tailed t-test: p = 0.02.
stem: Q12d. Is the result clinically significant? Statistically significant?

options.label: A
options.text: Not clinically significant, not statistically significant.
options.desc: p = 0.02 IS statistically significant. The bar graph shows a tiny difference — but the p-value alone would suggest it is not clinically meaningful. However the actual data shows 58% vs 17%, not the trivial gap this bar graph suggests.

options.label: B
options.text: Not clinically significant, but statistically significant.
options.desc: p = 0.02 < 0.05 = statistically significant. But is 5 extra pain-free joints clinically meaningful? The bar graph shows a moderate gap. 7/12 = 58% vs 2/12 = 17%. Many clinicians would call this clinically significant, making this answer arguable but not the NBME intended choice.

options.label: C
options.text: Clinically significant, but not statistically significant.
options.desc: p = 0.02 means statistically significant. This option reverses the boolean. The bar graph shows a real gap. p < 0.05 = reject null. Whether the gap is large enough to matter clinically is a separate judgment — but the statistical piece is settled.

options.label: D
options.text: Clinically significant AND statistically significant.
options.desc: Statistical: p = 0.02 < 0.05. Clinical: 7/12 (58%) vs 2/12 (17%) = 41pp absolute improvement. A large absolute difference in a disease where inflamed joints cause daily pain and disability. NBME answer key: both clinically and statistically significant. The effect size is substantial, and the p-value confirms it is unlikely to be noise.

options.label: E
options.text: Cannot determine clinical significance — the study did not pre-specify MCID.
options.desc: MCID is formally defined in some protocols, but NBME expects clinical judgment. The bar graph shows a large gap. 5 additional pain-free joints out of 12 inflamed at baseline is intuitively meaningful. NBME does not require pre-registered MCID to answer — they test your ability to distinguish statistical detectability from clinical worth.

explanation: p = 0.02 < 0.05 = statistically significant. 7/12 vs 2/12 = 41pp absolute improvement = clinically significant. NBME considers a 3.5x improvement in a disease with 12 inflamed joints at baseline to be clinically meaningful.
trap: Two separate questions, always: (1) Is p < 0.05? (2) Is the absolute difference large enough to matter? Tiny difference + large N = statistically significant but NOT clinically significant. Large difference + small N = clinically significant but NOT statistically significant. Both dimensions independently matter.

ad: RCT: new osteoporosis drug vs placebo in 300 women aged 40-60. At 5 years: bone density unchanged in drug group, decreased 2% in placebo (p = 0.01). Investigators conclude the drug decreases fracture risk.
stem: Q12e. What is the most appropriate conclusion about this claim?

options.label: A
options.text: Bone density is a surrogate endpoint — the trial measured bone density, not fractures.
options.desc: The drug preserved DEXA scores. That proves bone density maintenance — not fracture prevention. The bar graph shows equal clinical-event rates — because fractures were never measured. DEXA T-scores correlate with fracture risk at the population level, but a drug that improves DEXA may not reduce fractures. Bone could be denser but more brittle. Surrogates require separate validation trials.

options.label: B
options.text: Confounding — the treatment group may have had better baseline bone health.
options.desc: Randomization controls for confounding. The bar graph shows the observed effect. If the treatment group had better bones at baseline, the data would OVERestimate benefit — but the observed result (stable density on drug, decline on placebo) is internally consistent with a biological effect. The problem is endpoint validity, not internal validity.

options.label: C
options.text: The stable bone density suggests non-adherence — patients did not take the drug, producing a null result.
options.desc: Stable on drug while placebo declined = POSITIVE result for the surrogate. p = 0.01 confirms the between-group difference. The bar graph would show zero if non-adherence erased all effect. The drug DID maintain bone density — the issue is whether that finding MEANS anything for fractures.

options.label: D
options.text: Women under 40 were excluded — the population is too narrow to evaluate long-term benefit.
options.desc: Osteoporosis trials appropriately target postmenopausal women. Excluding premenopausal women is not a limitation — it is the relevant population. The bar graph shows the same effect. The real limitation is the surrogate endpoint, not the age range.

options.label: E
options.text: Selection bias — enrolling from gynecology clinics limits generalizability to the broader population.
options.desc: Gynecology clinics are where DEXA screening happens. The bar graph shows the same effect. Randomization ensures internal validity regardless of recruitment source. The question is about ENDPOINT validity — did they measure what matters? — not about representativeness.

explanation: Surrogate endpoint fallacy: bone density does not equal fractures. The trial proved the drug preserves bone on DEXA — it did NOT prove patients break fewer bones. To claim fracture prevention, you must measure fractures. The single most common flaw in drug advertising: claiming clinical benefit from biomarker changes.
trap: Biomarker does not equal clinical outcome. DEXA does not equal fewer fractures. Tumor shrinkage does not equal longer survival. Lower HbA1c does not equal fewer MIs. Always ask: did they measure what patients care about, or a lab value? NBME punishes accepting surrogate claims as clinical proof.

ad: Two rapid influenza tests (A and B, 10-minute results) were compared using ROC curves. The clinic currently waits 90 minutes for PCR.
stem: Q12f. Based on the ROC curves, Test A is more accurate than Test B in which range?

options.label: A
options.text: High false-positive rate range — Test A is higher on the right side, better sensitivity when specificity is sacrificed.
options.desc: Right side of ROC = high FPR, high sensitivity. If you tolerate many false positives, Test A catches more true cases. The bar graph shows higher sensitivity. Useful for outbreak screening where missing a case is worse than over-calling. But the NBME question asks about a SPECIFIC region where Test A outperforms.

options.label: B
options.text: All ranges — Test A is uniformly better, making it the superior test at every threshold.
options.desc: If Test A dominated everywhere, the ROC curves would not cross or separate by region. The bar graph shows difference. The NBME question describes curves with different shapes in different regions — meaning each test excels in a different clinical scenario. Uniform superiority is incorrect.

options.label: C
options.text: Low false-positive rate range — Test A curve rises steepest near the left axis, giving highest sensitivity at high specificity.
options.desc: Left side of ROC equals screening. Steep early rise = high sensitivity while keeping false positives low. The bar graph shows Test A with higher sensitivity at low FPR. This is ideal for low-prevalence screening where you want to minimize false alarms while catching most true cases. Test A dominates in this clinical niche.

options.label: D
options.text: Low sensitivity range — Test B is superior in that region, so Test A has no clinical advantage anywhere.
options.desc: If Test B is better at low sensitivity and Test A at low FPR, they serve different clinical purposes. The bar graph shows Test B higher in this range. Test A for screening (low FPR), Test B for ruling out disease (high sensitivity). The question asks where Test A is more accurate — and the low-FPR range IS Test A strength.

options.label: E
options.text: Cannot be determined — ROC curves show discrimination only, not calibration or clinical utility at specific thresholds.
options.desc: Discrimination IS what ROC measures — and you CAN read test performance at specific operating points from the curve. The bar graph shows equal rates — wrong. The curve directly shows sensitivity at each FPR. Calibration is a separate test characteristic, not a reason to ignore the ROC comparison.

explanation: ROC reading by region: left side (low FPR) = high-specificity screening. The curve with steeper rise near left axis excels at finding cases without over-calling. Test A dominates in the low-FPR range — correct for screening scenarios.
trap: Two ROC regions have different clinical meanings. Left = screening (minimize false positives). Right = case-finding (maximize sensitivity, accept false positives). A test that dominates in one region is not universally better. Read curves by region.

ad: A minimal-risk research study has low enrollment among African American patients. Interim IRB review confirms the disparity.
stem: Q12g. What is the best course of action to address this recruitment disparity?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask the IRB to waive informed consent — it appears to be deterring potential participants.
options.desc: Waiving consent because a minority group is reluctant to enroll is ethically indefensible. The bar graph shows zero participation. Informed consent protects ALL participants. Removing it selectively for hesitant groups compounds the historical exploitation that created the mistrust. Hard no.

options.label: B
options.text: Convene a focus group of potential participants to understand the reasons for reluctance.
options.desc: Community engagement is first-line for recruitment disparities. Listen before acting. The bar graph shows equal participation — the goal. Historical mistrust (Tuskegee, Henrietta Lacks) is real and well-documented. Understanding specific concerns allows targeted solutions: community health workers, trusted messengers, culturally appropriate materials. This is the NBME-approved answer pattern.

options.label: C
options.text: Focus recruitment on White patients who enroll more readily and acknowledge the limitation in the publication.
options.desc: Acknowledging a limitation does not fix it. The bar graph shows the disparity. Producing evidence that only applies to White populations is scientifically weak AND ethically problematic. "We will mention it in limitations" is not a solution — it is an admission of failure.

options.label: D
options.text: Recognize this as unavoidable and continue recruitment unchanged.
options.desc: Unavoidable is almost never true. The bar graph shows persistent disparity. Transportation, childcare, language, trust, cultural concordance, study burden — all addressable barriers. Declaring the problem unsolvable without trying is not acceptable.

options.label: E
options.text: Require all patients to participate in the study to receive care at this clinic.
options.desc: Coercion: tying clinical care to research participation. The bar graph shows forced equal rates — achieved unethically. Voluntariness is a fundamental ethical principle. Even if it produces representative data, the means undermine the end.

explanation: Community-based participatory research: when disparities emerge, engage the community. Focus groups, advisory boards, culturally tailored strategies. Never waive consent, never coerce, never accept exclusion. The ethical response is to understand and adapt.
trap: Recruitment disparities → community engagement, NOT coercion, NOT acceptance, NOT waiver of protections. NBME consistently tests this: listen first, adapt second, never remove protections. Applies across all dimensions of diversity.

ad: Essepro XL: once-daily stimulant for ADHD in patients 6-17. Contraindicated in structural cardiac abnormalities. A 19-year-old college student with no ADHD wants it for concentration. She has asthma, BMI 30, and a midsystolic click on exam.
stem: Q12h. Why should the physician NOT prescribe Essepro XL for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Contraindicated — interaction with asthma medications (albuterol, fluticasone, pseudoephedrine).
options.desc: No direct contraindication with asthma medications is listed in the ad. The bar graph shows equal rates. While stimulants can raise heart rate, the simplest, most direct reason is: the drug treats ADHD, and this patient does not have ADHD. Do not overcomplicate with drug interactions when the indication is absent.

options.label: B
options.text: Midsystolic click suggests mitral valve prolapse — a structural cardiac abnormality, which is a listed contraindication.
options.desc: Mitral valve prolapse IS a structural abnormality and IS listed as a contraindication. The bar graph shows equal rates. This is a valid medical reason. But NBME drug-ad questions reward the MOST DIRECT answer from the ad — and "not indicated" beats "relative contraindication found through physical exam" when the primary issue is no diagnosis.

options.label: C
options.text: Essepro XL is not indicated — the patient has no ADHD diagnosis.
options.desc: The drug treats ADHD. She does not have ADHD. Therefore: not indicated. The bar graph shows zero indication. This is the cleanest answer directly from the ad own language. She is seeking performance enhancement, not treatment for a diagnosed condition. Prescribing without indication is the core problem.

options.label: D
options.text: The patient is likely to divert the drug to friends — she already obtained it from her roommate.
options.desc: Concern about future diversion is speculative. The bar graph shows zero. She disclosed the roommate drug openly — that is honesty, not diversion risk. You cannot refuse a prescription based on predicted future behavior without evidence. The primary clinical reason is lack of indication.

options.label: E
options.text: No evidence Essepro XL helps with weight loss — her stated secondary goal.
options.desc: The ad actually mentions appetite suppression as a known effect. The bar graph accounts for this. Weight loss concerns are secondary — using a stimulant primarily for weight loss in a non-ADHD patient is inappropriate regardless of efficacy.

explanation: Drug ad says: "Indicated for ADHD." Patient has no ADHD. The drug is not indicated. This is the most direct, defensible answer from the ad itself. While mitral valve prolapse is a valid contraindication, "not indicated" is cleaner — it does not require you to connect exam findings to the contraindications list.
trap: NBME drug-ad answers: (1) Check indications — does the patient have the condition? If no, you are done. (2) Check contraindications. (3) Check efficacy data. Start with number 1 — absence of indication ends the analysis.

ad: Essepro XL vs methylphenidate XL comparison table. Essepro XL: duration 12 hours, once-daily. Methylphenidate XL: duration 8 hours.
stem: Q12i. Based on the ad, what is the greatest advantage of Essepro XL over methylphenidate XL?

options.label: A
options.text: Less insomnia — Essepro XL causes insomnia in 18% vs 25% for methylphenidate XL.
options.desc: Insomnia rates are similar — not a clear advantage. The bar graph shows overlapping rates. Drug-ad comparisons require finding the one objective metric where the advertised drug clearly outperforms. Side-effect rates that overlap are not convincing differentiators.

options.label: B
options.text: Lower abuse potential — the extended-release formulation has less dependency risk.
options.desc: Ads emphasize what they want you to believe. The bar graph shows higher abuse potential — not the advantage the ad claims. Unless comparative dependency data is provided, this is marketing language, not evidence. NBME tests whether you can distinguish claims from data.

options.label: C
options.text: Fewer GI side effects — lower rates of nausea and decreased appetite.
options.desc: Decreased appetite at 22% is substantial. The bar graph shows worse GI tolerability. Unless the ad provides direct comparison data showing lower GI side-effect rates for Essepro XL, this is not the advantage.

options.label: D
options.text: Better academic performance — the ad shows improved GPA data for Essepro XL users.
options.desc: Ads promote. They do not provide balanced evidence. The bar graph shows no difference. Unless comparative academic performance data with p-values is provided, this is a claim — not evidence. Tempting because the patient is a student, but the question asks about the GREATEST advantage based on the AD.

options.label: E
options.text: Longer duration of action — 12 hours vs 8 hours covers the entire day with a single dose.
options.desc: 12 hours vs 8 hours = 50 percent longer coverage. The bar graph shows the clinical implication: one morning dose covers school/work plus evening activities. Duration is an objective pharmacokinetic parameter — hard data, not a marketing claim. This is the kind of factual, ad-supported advantage NBME rewards.

explanation: NBME drug-ad advantage questions: the correct answer is the OBJECTIVE, measurable parameter where the advertised drug clearly beats the comparator. Duration of action (12h vs 8h) is a pharmacokinetic fact. Side effects, abuse potential, and academic performance either lack comparative data or are subjective claims.
trap: Drug-ad advantage = objective metric where the drug wins. Dosing frequency, duration of action, route of administration. NOT "better tolerated," "improved quality of life," or "higher patient satisfaction" unless the ad shows the comparator number for that claim. No comparator data = no advantage.

ad: A pharmaceutical company is developing a new drug for acute myeloid leukemia. The molecule has been synthesized in the lab and tested in vitro. Researchers are now ready to begin human testing.
stem: Q13a. Which is assessed in Phase I of a clinical trial?

options.label: A
options.text: Efficacy and optimal dosing — the drug is given to a moderate number of patients with the target disease.
options.desc: Phase II assesses efficacy and dosing in patients. Phase I comes before that. The bar graph shows equal rates. Phase I does not test whether the drug works — it tests whether the drug is safe enough to proceed to efficacy testing.

options.label: B
options.text: Comparison with the current standard of care — patients are randomized to the new drug or the existing gold standard.
options.desc: Phase III compares the new drug to placebo or standard of care in a large randomized trial. The bar graph would show a treatment comparison. Phase I is much earlier — before you know if the drug works, you need to know if it is safe in humans.

options.label: C
options.text: Safety, toxicity, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics — a small number of healthy volunteers receive the drug.
options.desc: Phase I = first-in-human. Healthy volunteers (or sometimes patients). Small numbers. The goal: establish safety profile, determine how the body handles the drug (pharmacokinetics) and how the drug affects the body (pharmacodynamics). The bar graph shows flat rates because Phase I is not designed to detect efficacy signals.

options.label: D
options.text: Post-marketing surveillance — the drug is already approved and monitored for rare or long-term adverse effects.
options.desc: Phase IV occurs AFTER FDA approval. The drug is on the market, and rare or late-onset side effects that would not appear in clinical trials (too few patients, too short duration) are detected through voluntary reporting systems and long-term registries. The bar graph is unchanged because Phase IV is observational, not experimental.

options.label: E
options.text: Animal studies confirming the in vitro findings before any human exposure.
options.desc: Animal studies are PRECLINICAL, not Phase I. They happen before human testing begins. Phase I starts after preclinical data supports moving into humans. The bar graph is flat — preclinical data is a prerequisite, not a phase.

explanation: Phase I: small number of healthy volunteers (or patients for toxic drugs like chemotherapy). Assess: safety, toxicity, pharmacokinetics (ADME — absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion), pharmacodynamics. Phase II: patients, efficacy, dosing, side effects. Phase III: large RCT, comparison to placebo/SOC. Phase IV: post-marketing surveillance for rare/long-term effects.
trap: Mnemonic for trial phases: 1-Safe, 2-Efficacy, 3-Compare, 4-Surveillance. Phase I = healthy humans, Phase II = sick humans, Phase III = sick humans vs controls, Phase IV = everyone after approval.

ad: A study compares mean fasting blood glucose across three groups: patients with type 2 diabetes, patients with prediabetes, and healthy controls.
stem: Q13b. Which statistical test is most appropriate for comparing means across three or more groups?

options.label: A
options.text: Chi-square test — it compares percentages of categorical outcomes across groups.
options.desc: Chi-square compares proportions, not means. If you have categorical data (e.g., percent of patients who achieved HbA1c under 7% in each group), use chi-square. The bar graph shows equal rates. For continuous variables like blood glucose levels, chi-square is wrong — you need a test that compares means.

options.label: B
options.text: ANOVA — it compares means across three or more groups.
options.desc: ANOVA = ANalysis Of VAriance. Compares means of 3+ groups. The bar graph shows group means. The null hypothesis: all group means are equal. If p < 0.05, at least one group differs. Post-hoc tests then identify which specific pairs differ. One-way ANOVA = one categorical factor. Two-way ANOVA = two factors with interactions.

options.label: C
options.text: t-test — it compares means between EXACTLY two groups.
options.desc: t-test is for two groups ONLY. Unpaired (independent) t-test for two different groups. Paired t-test for the same subjects measured twice. The bar graph shows two means compared. But the question has THREE groups — diabetes, prediabetes, and controls. Running multiple t-tests across 3 groups inflates the familywise error rate.

options.label: D
options.text: Fisher's exact test — it is the most precise test for small sample sizes with continuous data.
options.desc: Fisher's exact test is for CATEGORICAL data in 2x2 tables with small sample sizes. It calculates the exact probability of the observed table configuration, rather than using chi-square approximation. The bar graph is flat. It does not compare means — it compares proportions.

options.label: E
options.text: Meta-analysis — it pools data from multiple studies to improve precision of the mean comparison.
options.desc: Meta-analysis is a STUDY DESIGN, not a statistical test. It pools summary data from multiple completed studies to produce a more precise overall estimate of effect size. The bar graph shows equal rates. You cannot perform a meta-analysis on data from a single three-group study.

explanation: Statistical test selection: 2 groups, continuous outcome → t-test. 3+ groups, continuous outcome → ANOVA. Categorical outcome → chi-square (or Fisher's exact for small samples). ANOVA tests whether any group mean differs from the others. If significant, post-hoc pairwise comparisons identify which groups differ.
trap: Test selection algorithm: (1) What type of outcome? Continuous → t/ANOVA. Categorical → chi-square/Fisher. (2) How many groups? 2 → t-test. 3+ → ANOVA. (3) If categorical: 2x2 with small n → Fisher's. Larger → chi-square. Never run multiple t-tests for >2 groups — use ANOVA to control familywise error rate.

ad: A new biomarker for COPD is normally distributed in the population with mean = 100 mg/dL and SD = 20 mg/dL. Patients with values below 60 mg/dL are considered screen-positive. Reference: 68% of values fall within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, and 99.7% within 3 SD of the mean.
stem: Q13c. What percentage of the population would screen positive at this cutoff?

options.label: A
options.text: Under 1% — fewer than 1 in 100 individuals would test below 3 standard deviations from the mean.
options.desc: 3 SD below mean = 100 − 3×20 = 40. Only 0.15% of the population falls below 3 SD. The bar graph shows tiny proportions. The cutoff is 60, not 40. 99.7% of values are within 3 SD, so 0.15% are below 3 SD. That's not the right threshold for this question.

options.label: B
options.text: 2.5% — the cutoff at 2 standard deviations below the mean captures the bottom 2.5 percent of the distribution.
options.desc: 60 = 100 − 2×20 = 2 SD below the mean. 95% of values fall within 2 SD, leaving 5% outside — 2.5% above and 2.5% below. The bar graph shows approximately 2.5% screen-positive. If the disease prevalence in the general population is also around 2.5%, this cutoff makes clinical sense.

options.label: C
options.text: 5% — the bottom 5 percent of the population falls below this threshold.
options.desc: 5% = 1.645 SD below the mean, approximately. The bar graph shows 5% — double the correct value. The cutoff at 60 is 2 SD below, not 1.645 SD. 2 SD captures 2.5% on each tail, not 5%.

options.label: D
options.text: 16% — approximately 1 in 6 individuals would screen positive.
options.desc: 16% = 1 SD below the mean. The bar graph shows a much larger screen-positive population. 68% within 1 SD means 32% outside — 16% above, 16% below. But the cutoff is 60 (2 SD below), not 80 (1 SD below). Different threshold.

options.label: E
options.text: 34% — the proportion within 1 SD is 68 percent, so half of that, 34 percent, falls below the mean.
options.desc: 34% is the proportion between the mean and 1 SD below — not below 2 SD. The bar graph shows the wrong tail. The question asks for those BELOW 60 (2 SD down), not between the mean and 1 SD down. This confuses the area under the curve.

explanation: Normal distribution rule: 68-95-99.7. 60 mg/dL = 100 − 2×20 = 2 SD below the mean. 95% within 2 SD → 5% outside → 2.5% below 2 SD and 2.5% above. Therefore approximately 2.5% screen positive.
trap: 68-95-99.7 rule: 1 SD = 68% (34% each side), 2 SD = 95% (47.5% each side), 3 SD = 99.7%. To find the percentage beyond k SD: calculate (100% − within-k-SD%) / 2 for one tail. For 2 SD: (100 − 95) / 2 = 2.5%.

ad: Drug X vs placebo in type 2 diabetes RCT. Results: Drug X lowers blood glucose with p = 0.03, α = 0.05, power = 80%.
stem: Q13d. Which conclusion can most likely be drawn from α = 0.05 and power = 80%?

options.label: A
options.text: There is a 3% chance these results occurred by chance if the alternative hypothesis is true.
options.desc: p-value is the probability of observing results this extreme if the NULL hypothesis is true — not the alternative. The bar graph shows the p-value. If the null were true (no difference), there is a 3% chance of seeing a result like this or more extreme. That is what p = 0.03 means. The alternative hypothesis has nothing to do with p-value calculation.

options.label: B
options.text: There is a 97% chance the null hypothesis is false.
options.desc: p-value does NOT equal the probability that the null is false. The bar graph is flat because this statement is a fundamental misinterpretation. p = 0.03 means P(data | null is true) = 0.03, NOT P(null is false | data). These are different conditional probabilities. You cannot flip the direction of a conditional probability without using Bayes' theorem.

options.label: C
options.text: There is a 3% chance a Type I error occurred.
options.desc: Type I error probability = α, not p-value. The bar graph shows the same number but means something different. α = 0.05 means: IF the null is true, there is a 5% chance of rejecting it. Once you HAVE rejected (p < α), the post-hoc probability of Type I error is not simply α or p. The p-value does not represent error probability.

options.label: D
options.text: There is a 5% chance a Type I error occurred if the null hypothesis were true.
options.desc: α = probability of Type I error WHEN the null is true. The bar graph shows 5%. This is the correct interpretation: before the study, we set a 5% risk of falsely rejecting a true null. Once we observe p = 0.03 and reject, we cannot say "the probability a Type I error occurred is 5%." But the design-level interpretation is: under the null, 5% of such studies would produce false rejections.

options.label: E
options.text: There is a 20% chance a Type II error may occur over many repeated studies.
options.desc: β = 1 − power = 1 − 0.80 = 0.20 = 20%. The bar graph shows 20%. This is correct: power of 80% means IF a true effect of the specified size exists, 80% of studies will detect it — and 20% will miss it (Type II error). Over many repeated studies, a Type II error will occur in 20% of replications.

explanation: α = 0.05 means: 5% chance of Type I error (false positive) if the null is true. Power = 80% means: 80% chance of correctly rejecting a false null. β = 1 − power = 20% chance of Type II error (false negative) when a true effect exists. The p-value (0.03) is NOT the probability of error — it is the probability of the observed data (or more extreme) assuming the null is true.
trap: Three independent numbers: (1) p-value = compatibility of data with null, NOT error probability. (2) α = pre-set Type I error rate. (3) β = 1−power = Type II error rate. The most common UW/NBME trap: equating p-value with Type I error probability. They are different concepts.

ad: A ferritin test with a cutoff of 20 ng/mL is used to screen for GI malignancies. After a year, the cutoff is raised to 50 ng/mL. The disease is characterized by low ferritin levels.
stem: Q13e. What happens to sensitivity and specificity when the cutoff is raised from 20 to 50 ng/mL?

options.label: A
options.text: Sensitivity increases, specificity decreases — more patients screen positive, catching more true cases but generating more false alarms.
options.desc: Raising the cutoff makes the test MORE inclusive. The bar graph: higher sensitivity, lower specificity. Everyone with ferritin between 20 and 50 who was previously negative is now positive. This catches more true cases (higher sensitivity) but also labels more healthy people as positive (lower specificity). Screening benefits, confirmatory suffers.

options.label: B
options.text: Sensitivity and specificity both increase — the higher cutoff better separates diseased from healthy.
options.desc: Sensitivity and specificity have an inverse relationship when you shift the cutoff. The bar graph shows both high — impossible. You cannot improve both simultaneously by moving a threshold on the same test. The ROC curve shows the trade-off. Moving one way improves sensitivity, moving the other improves specificity. Never both.

options.label: C
options.text: Sensitivity decreases, specificity increases — the test becomes more selective, missing some true cases but reducing false positives.
options.desc: Wrong direction. The bar graph shows the opposite of what happens. Raising the cutoff from 20 to 50 means MORE people test positive (lower = positive for this disease). So sensitivity goes UP (fewer false negatives) and specificity goes DOWN (more false positives). You described the effect of making the test MORE restrictive — which would be LOWERING the cutoff in this disease.

options.label: D
options.text: Both are unchanged — sensitivity and specificity are fixed properties of a test.
options.desc: Sensitivity and specificity are fixed properties at a GIVEN cutoff — change the cutoff, change the properties. The bar graph shows stability — but the cutoff changed. For any diagnostic test with a continuous measurement, sensitivity and specificity vary with the threshold. PPV and NPV also vary because they depend on population prevalence.

options.label: E
options.text: Sensitivity increases, specificity is unchanged — the test identifies more true cases without affecting the false-positive rate.
options.desc: Raising the cutoff captures more positives of both types: true and false. The bar graph shows sensitivity increasing while specificity stays flat. But when you call more people positive, you INEVITABLY include some healthy people you previously called negative. Specificity must decline. The two metrics move in opposite directions when the threshold changes.

explanation: For a disease where LOW values = positive, raising the cutoff (from 20 to 50) means MORE people test positive. Sensitivity goes UP (fewer false negatives — you catch those between 20–50 who were previously missed). Specificity goes DOWN (more false positives — healthy people with ferritin 20–50 are now labeled positive).
trap: Cutoff shift rule: Making the test MORE inclusive (calling more people positive) → sensitivity UP, specificity DOWN. Making the test MORE restrictive (calling fewer people positive) → sensitivity DOWN, specificity UP. Think of it as a net — wider net catches more fish (true positives) but also more debris (false positives).

ad: A new anti-melanoma drug improves average survival by 2 years with minimal serious side effects. It is approved and released to market. Three years later, case reports emerge of patients developing seizures on the drug — a side effect NOT observed in the initial trials.
stem: Q13f. What is the most appropriate response to this post-marketing finding?

options.label: A
options.text: Withdraw the drug from the market until further analysis is completed.
options.desc: Serious unexpected adverse events detected in Phase IV warrant market withdrawal pending investigation. The bar graph shows zero use during investigation. The drug proved efficacy in Phase III, but Phase IV (post-marketing surveillance) exists precisely because rare or long-term effects that Phase III could not detect (too few patients, too short follow-up) now emerge. Patient safety takes priority.

options.label: B
options.text: Change the recommended dosage of the drug — the seizures are likely dose-dependent.
options.desc: Without data on dose-response for seizures, lowering the dose is guessing. The bar graph shows continued use at a different dose. Dose reduction might also reduce efficacy — and the disease is advanced melanoma. You would need a new trial to determine if a lower dose is both effective AND seizure-free. Withdraw first, study second.

options.label: C
options.text: Add an anti-epileptic drug to the standard regimen for all patients.
options.desc: Adding a second drug to every patient to prevent a rare side effect? That is polypharmacy without evidence. The bar graph shows dual therapy. Anti-epileptics have their own side effects. You do not add drugs preemptively to prevent rare adverse events — you withdraw the offending drug and investigate.

options.label: D
options.text: Change the target population — only patients without seizure history should receive the drug.
options.desc: Narrowing the population might miss the real problem. The bar graph shows restricted use. The case reports do not specify whether seizures occurred only in patients with pre-existing risk factors. Changing labels without understanding the mechanism is premature. First, determine WHY seizures occur — then decide if a subpopulation can safely use the drug.

options.label: E
options.text: Administer the drug only in the ICU where seizures can be promptly managed.
options.desc: Chemotherapy for advanced melanoma is not administered in the ICU. The bar graph shows an impractical setting. Moving chronic cancer treatment to a critical care unit for a rare side effect would be an enormous burden on patients and the healthcare system. If a drug requires ICU administration for routine use, it is not safe for market.

explanation: Phase IV = post-marketing surveillance. Purpose: detect rare or long-term adverse effects that Phase III trials (typically a few thousand patients over months to a few years) cannot capture. When a serious, unexpected signal emerges — seizures in this case — the appropriate first step is to withdraw the drug pending investigation. This is exactly what happened with drugs like rofecoxib (Vioxx) and many others.
trap: Drug safety hierarchy: Phase I = is it safe? Phase II = does it work? Phase III = is it better? Phase IV = are there rare problems? If Phase IV finds a life-threatening signal, the answer is ALWAYS: withdraw, investigate, re-evaluate. Never: lower dose, add a second drug, restrict population, or move to ICU.

ad: A meta-analysis on alcohol and liver cirrhosis produces results that differ significantly from the widely accepted literature. 12 studies were pooled.
stem: Q13g. What is the most likely explanation for discrepant meta-analysis results?

options.label: A
options.text: The relationship between alcohol and liver cirrhosis has changed recently — newer data supersedes older findings.
options.desc: Biological relationships between established risk factors and disease do not change over time. The bar graph shows equal rates. Alcohol's hepatotoxicity is a stable biological fact. If new studies contradict decades of consistent evidence, the more likely explanation is that something is wrong with the new analysis — not that biology changed.

options.label: B
options.text: All previous theories were wrong — the meta-analysis pooled enough data to overturn the consensus.
options.desc: One meta-analysis overturning a mountain of consistent evidence is far more likely to be flawed than revolutionary. The bar graph is flat. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. When one analysis contradicts dozens of prior studies, the burden of proof is on the new analysis to demonstrate its methodological superiority — not on the prior literature to defend itself.

options.label: C
options.text: There may be a non-linear relationship — alcohol has different effects at different doses, averaging out to zero.
options.desc: A non-linear (J-shaped or U-shaped) relationship could explain heterogeneity, but the stem says results DIFFER from accepted findings. The bar graph shows a possible non-linear pattern. A non-linear relationship would produce systematic patterns, not an entirely different conclusion. This is a distraction answer for the real issue.

options.label: D
options.text: The researcher used low-quality or biased studies — meta-analysis quality depends entirely on the quality of included studies.
options.desc: Garbage in, garbage out. Meta-analysis amplifies bias if it pools biased studies. The bar graph shows flat rates — the average of garbage is still garbage. A meta-analysis is only as good as the studies it includes. If inclusion criteria are too loose or low-quality studies dominate, the pooled estimate will be wrong. The most common reason for meta-analysis results that contradict the broader literature is poor study selection or methodological flaws.

options.label: E
options.text: Meta-analyses typically have low statistical power — the discrepancy is due to random sampling error.
options.desc: Meta-analysis INCREASES power by pooling samples across studies. The bar graph is flat. This is the opposite of the truth. The main advantage of meta-analysis is that combining multiple studies dramatically increases sample size and precision. Low power is a problem for individual small studies — meta-analysis solves precisely that problem.

explanation: Meta-analysis quality = quality of included studies. If the pooled studies are biased, have confounding, use different definitions, or have poor methodology, the meta-analysis will produce biased results. Key threats: publication bias (negative studies missing), heterogeneity (studies too different to combine), and poor-quality primary studies.
trap: Meta-analysis checklist: (1) Are inclusion criteria appropriate? (2) Do the pooled studies measure the same thing? (3) Was publication bias assessed (funnel plot)? (4) If results contradict the literature, suspect poor study selection — not that "everything we knew was wrong."

ad: A researcher surveys 100 patients with osteoarthritis about their pain scores (range 0-100, sum of 10 sub-scales). 98 patients score between 20-50. Two patients score 100.
stem: Q13h. Which measure of central tendency is MOST affected by these two extreme values?

options.label: A
options.text: Mode — the most frequent value shifts dramatically when extreme outliers appear.
options.desc: Mode is the LEAST affected by outliers. The bar graph shows stability. Even with two patients scoring 100, 98 others fall between 20-50. The most frequent value remains within 20-50. Mode only changes if the outlier becomes the most common value — which requires many more outliers than 2 out of 100.

options.label: B
options.text: Mean — the arithmetic average is pulled toward the extreme values.
options.desc: Mean = sum / n. Two scores of 100 add 200 to the sum when the rest are much lower. The bar graph shows a rightward shift. If the 98 patients average 35, the sum = 98×35 + 2×100 = 3,430 + 200 = 3,630. Mean = 36.3. Without outliers: 98×35 = 3,430, mean = 35.0. The two outliers dragged the mean up by 1.3 points — more than any other measure.

options.label: C
options.text: Median — the middle value shifts because the extreme values change the ordering.
options.desc: Median is LESS affected by outliers. The bar graph shows a small shift. In 100 sorted values, the median is the 50th value. Adding two extreme values at the top does NOT change which value is in the middle — unless there are so many outliers that the center shifts. With 98 regular values and 2 outliers, the median barely budges.

options.label: D
options.text: All three are equally affected — outliers change the entire distribution.
options.desc: Outliers affect mean, median, and mode to DIFFERENT degrees. The bar graph shows equal effect — false. Mean > median > mode in sensitivity to outliers. A single extreme value can substantially change the mean but barely register in the median and not affect the mode at all. Understanding this relationship is critical for choosing the right summary statistic.

options.label: E
options.text: None is affected — measures of central tendency are robust to outliers by definition.
options.desc: Measures of central tendency are NOT robust to outliers — especially the mean. The bar graph shows no change — incorrect. "Robust" in statistics means resistant to outliers. The median is considered robust. The mean is NOT robust. If you want a central tendency measure that outliers won't distort, report the median — not the mean.

explanation: Sensitivity to outliers: mean > median > mode. Mean is calculated from ALL values, so extreme observations pull it directly. Median only cares about the middle position. Mode only cares about frequency. Right-skewed data (positive outliers) shows: mode < median < mean.
trap: For skewed data, report the MEDIAN. The mean misleads — a few high rollers inflate the "average." Right skew: mode < median < mean (tail points right). Left skew: mean < median < mode (tail points left). When you hear "average household income" vs "median household income" — median is almost always the honest number.

ad: COVID-19 has affected 10,000 people in a population of 100,000. A total of 100 infected patients died from the disease.
stem: Q13i. What is the case fatality rate?

options.label: A
options.text: 0.1% — the proportion of the total population that died from the disease.
options.desc: That is the population mortality rate: 100 deaths / 100,000 population = 0.1%. The bar graph shows deaths per population. But case fatality rate is different: it is deaths among those who contracted the disease, not deaths among the entire population. Different denominator.

options.label: B
options.text: 1% — 100 deaths among 10,000 affected individuals.
options.desc: Case fatality rate = deaths from the disease / total cases × 100. The bar graph shows 1%. 100 / 10,000 = 0.01 = 1%. This tells you: if a patient contracts COVID-19, what is the probability they die from it? CFR answers the question "how deadly is this disease once you get it?".

options.label: C
options.text: 10% — the proportion of the affected population relative to total cases.
options.desc: 10% would be 1,000 deaths among 10,000 cases — or 100 deaths among 1,000 cases. The bar graph shows a much higher CFR. The actual data: 100 deaths / 10,000 cases = 1%. This confuses the prevalence (10,000/100,000 = 10%) with the case fatality rate.

options.label: D
options.text: 15% — the daily case rate multiplied by the mortality proportion.
options.desc: Daily case rate has nothing to do with case fatality rate. The bar graph shows 15% — incorrect. CFR = deaths / cases. Period. Not rate × mortality proportion. Not daily incidence × something. Simple ratio.

options.label: E
options.text: Cannot be determined because we do not know the incidence rate.
options.desc: Case fatality rate does not require incidence. The bar graph shows zero — undetermined. CFR = number of deaths from the disease / number of people with the disease. Both numbers are given: 100 and 10,000. Incidence would tell you about new cases, which is a different question entirely.

explanation: Case Fatality Rate (CFR) = (deaths from disease / total cases) × 100. 100 / 10,000 = 1%. CFR measures disease severity. Do not confuse with: mortality rate (deaths / total population), incidence (new cases / population at risk), or prevalence (existing cases / total population).
trap: Four rates, four denominators: (1) CFR = deaths ÷ cases (how deadly is the disease?), (2) Mortality rate = deaths ÷ population (how many people die from it?), (3) Attack rate = cases ÷ exposed population (how contagious?), (4) Incidence = new cases ÷ population at risk (how fast is it spreading?).

ad: A retrospective cohort study of long-term aspirin use and colorectal cancer reports: RR = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.76 to 0.96. A second center replicates the study but reports: RR = 0.87, 95% CI: 0.70 to 1.15. They note significant loss to follow-up, mostly among patients NOT taking aspirin.
stem: Q13j. What bias is most likely affecting the second center's results?

options.label: A
options.text: Recall bias — participants who develop cancer are more likely to overreport their aspirin use when asked retrospectively.
options.desc: This is a COHORT study — exposure (aspirin use) is determined at baseline, not by patient recall. The bar graph is flat. Recall bias affects case-control studies where participants are asked to remember past exposures. Here, the problem is loss to follow-up, not faulty memory.

options.label: B
options.text: Observer bias — the researchers' belief that aspirin is protective influenced how they interpreted outcomes.
options.desc: Observer bias = researcher expectations affect outcome assessment. The bar graph shows potential bias. But the stem explicitly describes loss to follow-up from the non-aspirin group — this is a sampling problem, not a measurement or interpretation problem. Blinding prevents observer bias. Attrition is a different issue.

options.label: C
options.text: Lead-time bias — early detection of colorectal cancer in the aspirin group makes survival appear longer than it actually is.
options.desc: Lead-time bias = screening detects disease earlier, making survival APPEAR longer without actually changing the disease course. The bar graph is flat. This study is about CANCER INCIDENCE (RR = relative risk of developing cancer), not survival time. Lead-time bias affects survival endpoints, not incidence outcomes.

options.label: D
options.text: Attrition bias (a form of selection bias) — uneven loss to follow-up disproportionately removes non-aspirin users, distorting the risk estimate.
options.desc: When more patients in one group drop out, the remaining sample is no longer comparable. The bar graph shows reduced precision — the CI now includes 1. If non-aspirin users who stayed were systematically healthier (or sicker) than those who left, the RR is biased. Uneven attrition destroys randomization by making the groups different at the end than they were at the start.

options.label: E
options.text: Length-time bias — aspirin users have slower-growing cancers that are more likely to be detected during the study period.
options.desc: Length-time bias applies to SCREENING studies, not cohort studies of incidence. The bar graph is flat. Length-time bias occurs when screening preferentially detects slow-growing diseases because fast-growing ones present and kill between screening intervals. This study is following patients for colorectal cancer DEVELOPMENT, not screening for existing cancers.

explanation: Attrition bias (loss to follow-up bias) is a form of selection bias. When participants are lost disproportionately from one group — and those lost are different from those who remain — the groups are no longer comparable. The CI widening from 0.76-0.96 to 0.70-1.15 reflects both reduced sample size and potential bias from differential loss.
trap: Bias identification by study design: Case-control → recall bias. Cohort → attrition/loss to follow-up. Screening studies → lead-time, length-time. Any study with faulty equipment → measurement bias. Any study where researchers know group assignment → observer bias. Match the bias to the study's vulnerability.

ad: A researcher studying second-hand smoke and aortic aneurysm needs to present results in 6 months. She wants to calculate relative risk: risk of aneurysm in exposed vs unexposed individuals.
stem: Q13k. Which study design is BEST suited to her goal AND timeline?

options.label: A
options.text: Prospective cohort study — follow exposed and unexposed groups forward for aneurysm development.
options.desc: Prospective cohort = forward in time from exposure to outcome. The bar graph shows equal rates. This is the ideal design for calculating relative risk. But the timeline is the problem: the researcher has 6 MONTHS, and aortic aneurysms take years to develop. A prospective cohort study would need a decade or more.

options.label: B
options.text: Case-control study — identify aneurysm patients and matched controls, then determine exposure history.
options.desc: Case-control = start with outcome, look back at exposure. Good for rare diseases. The bar graph shows flat rates. But the researcher wants RELATIVE RISK, and case-control studies calculate ODDS RATIO, not relative risk. In rare diseases OR ≈ RR, but the stem specifically says "relative risk" — and case-control cannot directly calculate it.

options.label: C
options.text: Retrospective cohort study — identify exposed and unexposed groups from the past and determine who developed aneurysms by the present.
options.desc: Retrospective cohort = exposure status determined from PAST records, outcomes assessed in the PRESENT. The bar graph shows relative risk directly: 0.15 / 0.05 = 3.0. Both exposed and unexposed are already known from historical data. You just need to check who developed aneurysms. This can be done in 6 months because you are not waiting for events — they already happened.

options.label: D
options.text: Clinical trial — randomly assign participants to second-hand smoke exposure vs clean air and measure aneurysm rates.
options.desc: Randomly exposing humans to second-hand smoke is unethical. The bar graph cannot exist because the trial cannot ethically exist. You cannot randomize people to a known carcinogen. This question tests both study design knowledge and ethical reasoning.

options.label: E
options.text: Cross-sectional study — survey a population about both smoke exposure and aneurysm diagnosis at one time point.
options.desc: Cross-sectional = snapshot. You can calculate prevalence, not relative risk. The bar graph shows equal rates — there is no temporal relationship. Relative risk requires knowing that exposure preceded outcome, which cross-sectional studies cannot establish. You measure both at the same time — no causality inference.

explanation: Retrospective cohort: use historical records to identify exposure groups, then assess outcomes that have already occurred by the present day. Much faster than prospective because you do not wait for events. The key difference from case-control: in a cohort study, you start with EXPOSURE and measure OUTCOME — which allows direct calculation of relative risk.
trap: Three study designs that calculate risk: (1) Prospective cohort → relative risk, gold standard, slow, expensive. (2) Retrospective cohort → relative risk, faster, relies on good historical records. (3) Case-control → odds ratio, good for rare diseases, cheapest. When speed matters, retrospective cohort beats prospective.

ad: 10 healthy volunteers are given a new drug. No serious side effects occur. The study also measured absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion.
stem: Q13l. After this phase succeeds, what happens NEXT in clinical trial progression?

options.label: A
options.text: Release the drug to the market with a Phase IV monitoring program.
options.desc: Phase IV is POST-approval. You cannot skip Phase II and III. The bar graph shows no prior efficacy data. A drug cannot reach the market after only Phase I safety testing in 10 healthy volunteers. You have not demonstrated it works in patients, at what dose, or that it beats placebo.

options.label: B
options.text: Give the drug to a moderate number of patients with the target disease to assess efficacy, dosing, and side effects.
options.desc: Phase II = first time the drug is given to PATIENTS with the disease. The bar graph shows effect exploration. After safety is established in healthy volunteers, the next logical step is: does the drug actually work in the people you intend to treat? Phase II determines optimal dosing, early efficacy signals, and common adverse effects in the target population.

options.label: C
options.text: Immediately compare the drug to the current standard of care in a large multicenter randomized controlled trial.
options.desc: Phase III = large RCT vs SOC/placebo. But you skipped Phase II. The bar graph shows comparison. You need to know the right dose and whether the drug shows enough promise to justify an expensive, large-scale trial. Phase II provides that information. Skipping it is scientifically and ethically inappropriate.

options.label: D
options.text: Return to preclinical testing in animals because human Phase I data was insufficient.
options.desc: Phase I succeeded — no serious side effects, pharmacokinetics are understood. The bar graph shows backward progression. Returning to animals after passing Phase I safety in humans would be a step backward. The data supports advancing to Phase II, not retreating to preclinical.

options.label: E
options.text: Perform another Phase I trial with 10 more healthy volunteers to confirm reproducibility.
options.desc: Repeating Phase I with 10 more volunteers adds no new information. The bar graph shows redundancy. Phase I determined safety and PK/PD in humans. Unless a safety signal emerged, repeating Phase I is unnecessary. The next logical step is to test the drug in the patients it is designed to help — at the right dose.

explanation: Clinical trial phases are sequential: Phase I (safety in healthy volunteers, 10-100 people) → Phase II (efficacy, dosing, side effects in patients, 100-300) → Phase III (large RCT vs SOC/placebo, 300-3,000+) → FDA approval → Phase IV (post-marketing surveillance, thousands+). Each phase builds on the previous. No skipping.
trap: Phase progression is a pipeline: I-Safe → II-Efficacy → III-Compare → FDA → IV-Surveillance. A drug CANNOT skip phases. The only exception is accelerated approval, which allows Phase II data for life-threatening diseases with no alternatives — but even then Phase III confirmatory trials are still required post-approval.

stem: 62-year-old male comes to the office for a check-up. He has no significant past medical history and currently feels fine. Last year his wife was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the colon. He is interested in the screening programs for colon cancer. Which of the following features of a test makes it valuable as a screening tool: high specificity high positive predictive value high sensitivity high accuracy high precision

options.text: high specificity
high positive predictive value
high sensitivity
high accuracy
high precision

explanation: The idea behind screening is to identify early cases of a disease. In order for a test to be a valuable screening test it needs to identify almost all individuals affected by a condition. As such, it is important that screening tests have the lowest possible false negative rate. The false positive rate is of lesser concern as individuals identified by screening tests can be further assessed by tests with higher specificity to confirm the diagnosis. Positive and negative predicted value tell us what proportion of positive and negative tests are true positives/negatives. Accurate tests are the ones that produce results that are close to the real value, while precise tests produce results that are close to each other.
trap: Screening = catch all cases (low FN). Sensitivity matters more than specificity

stem: A large medical center has developed a biomarker that can be used for ALS screening. They decide to offer the test to all patients aged over 50. Subsequently, they determine that following the introduction of the test, survival of ALS patients has increased by approximately two months. Which of the following is a possible explanation of the finding: selection bias measurement bias length-time bias lead-time bias

options.text: selection bias
measurement bias
length-time bias
lead-time bias
confounding

explanation: Lead-time bias refers to apparent survival increase due to earlier disease detection without any change in disease course. ALS is an incurable disease with very limited treatment options. Early treatment would be unlikely to alter the disease course. Selection bias refers to nonrandom sampling of study participants.
